# Contributing

## Use of AI

All use of AI in contributions must follow the
[AI Policy](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/blob/master/AI_POLICY.md).

Contributions not following the AI Policy will be closed.

ripgrep (rg)
------------
ripgrep is a line-oriented search tool that recursively searches the current
directory for a regex pattern. By default, ripgrep will respect gitignore rules
and automatically skip hidden files/directories and binary files. (To disable
all automatic filtering by default, use `rg -uuu`.) ripgrep has first class
support on Windows, macOS and Linux, with binary downloads available for [every
release](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/releases). ripgrep is similar to
other popular search tools like The Silver Searcher, ack and grep.

[![Build status](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/workflows/ci/badge.svg)](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/actions)
[![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/ripgrep.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/ripgrep)
[![Packaging status](https://repology.org/badge/tiny-repos/ripgrep.svg)](https://repology.org/project/ripgrep/badges)

Dual-licensed under MIT or the [UNLICENSE](https://unlicense.org).

Please see the [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md) for a release history.

### Quick examples comparing tools

This example searches the entire
[Linux kernel source tree](https://github.com/BurntSushi/linux)
(after running `make defconfig && make -j8`) for `[A-Z]+_SUSPEND`, where
all matches must be words. Timings were collected on a system with an Intel
i9-12900K 5.2 GHz.

Please remember that a single benchmark is never enough! See my
[blog post on ripgrep](https://blog.burntsushi.net/ripgrep/)
for a very detailed comparison with more benchmarks and analysis.

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep (Unicode) | `rg -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | **0.082s** (1.00x) |
| [hypergrep](https://github.com/p-ranav/hypergrep) | `hgrep -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.167s (2.04x) |
| [git grep](https://www.kernel.org/pub/software/scm/git/docs/git-grep.html) | `git grep -P -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.273s (3.34x) |
| [The Silver Searcher](https://github.com/ggreer/the_silver_searcher) | `ag -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 534 | 0.443s (5.43x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -r --ignore-files --no-hidden -I -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.639s (7.82x) |
| [git grep](https://www.kernel.org/pub/software/scm/git/docs/git-grep.html) | `LC_ALL=C git grep -E -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.727s (8.91x) |
| [git grep (Unicode)](https://www.kernel.org/pub/software/scm/git/docs/git-grep.html) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 git grep -E -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 2.670s (32.70x) |
| [ack](https://github.com/beyondgrep/ack3) | `ack -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 2677 | 2.935s (35.94x) |

Here's another benchmark on the same corpus as above that disregards gitignore
files and searches with a whitelist instead. The corpus is the same as in the
previous benchmark, and the flags passed to each command ensure that they are
doing equivalent work:

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep | `rg -uuu -tc -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 447 | **0.063s** (1.00x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -r -n --include='*.c' --include='*.h' -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 447 | 0.607s (9.62x) |
| [GNU grep](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `grep -E -r -n --include='*.c' --include='*.h' -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 447 | 0.674s (10.69x) |

Now we'll move to searching on single large file. Here is a straight-up
comparison between ripgrep, ugrep and GNU grep on a file cached in memory
(~13GB, [`OpenSubtitles.raw.en.gz`](https://object.pouta.csc.fi/OPUS-OpenSubtitles/v2018/mono/en.txt.gz), decompressed):

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep (Unicode) | `rg -w 'Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 7882 | **1.042s** (1.00x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -w 'Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 7882 | 1.339s (1.28x) |
| [GNU grep (Unicode)](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 egrep -w 'Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 7882 | 6.577s (6.31x) |

In the above benchmark, passing the `-n` flag (for showing line numbers)
increases the times to `1.664s` for ripgrep and `9.484s` for GNU grep. ugrep
times are unaffected by the presence or absence of `-n`.

Beware of performance cliffs though:

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep (Unicode) | `rg -w '[A-Z]\w+ Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 485 | **1.053s** (1.00x) |
| [GNU grep (Unicode)](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 grep -E -w '[A-Z]\w+ Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 485 | 6.234s (5.92x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -w '[A-Z]\w+ Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 485 | 28.973s (27.51x) |

And performance can drop precipitously across the board when searching big
files for patterns without any opportunities for literal optimizations:

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep | `rg '[A-Za-z]{30}'` | 6749 | **15.569s** (1.00x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -E '[A-Za-z]{30}'` | 6749 | 21.857s (1.40x) |
| [GNU grep](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=C grep -E '[A-Za-z]{30}'` | 6749 | 32.409s (2.08x) |
| [GNU grep (Unicode)](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 grep -E '[A-Za-z]{30}'` | 6795 | 8m30s (32.74x) |

Finally, high match counts also tend to both tank performance and smooth
out the differences between tools (because performance is dominated by how
quickly one can handle a match and not the algorithm used to detect the match,
generally speaking):

| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
| ripgrep | `rg the` | 83499915 | **6.948s** (1.00x) |
| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep the` | 83499915 | 11.721s (1.69x) |
| [GNU grep](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=C grep the` | 83499915 | 15.217s (2.19x) |

### Why should I use ripgrep?

* It can replace many use cases served by other search tools
  because it contains most of their features and is generally faster. (See
  [the FAQ](FAQ.md#posix4ever) for more details on whether ripgrep can truly
  replace grep.)
* Like other tools specialized to code search, ripgrep defaults to
  [recursive search](GUIDE.md#recursive-search) and does [automatic
  filtering](GUIDE.md#automatic-filtering). Namely, ripgrep won't search files
  ignored by your `.gitignore`/`.ignore`/`.rgignore` files, it won't search
  hidden files and it won't search binary files. Automatic filtering can be
  disabled with `rg -uuu`.
* ripgrep can [search specific types of files](GUIDE.md#manual-filtering-file-types).
  For example, `rg -tpy foo` limits your search to Python files and `rg -Tjs
  foo` excludes JavaScript files from your search. ripgrep can be taught about
  new file types with custom matching rules.
* ripgrep supports many features found in `grep`, such as showing the context
  of search results, searching multiple patterns, highlighting matches with
  color and full Unicode support. Unlike GNU grep, ripgrep stays fast while
  supporting Unicode (which is always on).
* ripgrep has optional support for switching its regex engine to use PCRE2.
  Among other things, this makes it possible to use look-around and
  backreferences in your patterns, which are not supported in ripgrep's default
  regex engine. PCRE2 support can be enabled with `-P/--pcre2` (use PCRE2
  always) or `--auto-hybrid-regex` (use PCRE2 only if needed). An alternative
  syntax is provided via the `--engine (default|pcre2|auto)` option.
* ripgrep has [rudimentary support for replacements](GUIDE.md#replacements),
  which permit rewriting output based on what was matched.

report.overview: ripgrep is a line-oriented recursive search tool (`rg`) written in Rust that walks a directory tree while respecting `.gitignore`/`.ignore` rules, matches each file with either Rust's `regex` crate or PCRE2, and prints results through one of three printers (standard/summary/JSON). The repository is a Cargo workspace: a thin binary crate at `crates/core` glues together ten reusable library crates (`grep-matcher`, `grep-regex`, `grep-pcre2`, `grep-searcher`, `grep-printer`, `grep-cli`, `ignore`, `globset`, plus the experimental `grep-index`), each published independently on crates.io. What is distinctive is the amount of engineering in the boring parts: a hand-rolled CLI parser over a 246KB table of `&dyn Flag` trait objects that also generates the man page, `--help` text and four shells' completions from the same source of truth; a directory walker that reimplements gitignore precedence with a parallel work-stealing traversal; and a searcher that chooses between memory maps, a reusable line buffer, and multi-line slice scanning per file. An unstable `unstable-index` feature adds a redb+fst ngram index behind `-X/--index` and `--x-crud`.

system_map.summary: The workspace root `Cargo.toml` declares the `ripgrep` package producing one binary `rg` from `crates/core/main.rs`, and lists ten workspace members under `crates/`. `crates/core` is not published as a library — it is pure glue plus the CLI definition, as its README states. Dependencies flow strictly downward: core → `grep` facade → `grep-searcher`/`grep-printer`/`grep-regex`/`grep-pcre2`/`grep-cli`/`grep-matcher`, with `ignore` and `globset` used for traversal and glob filtering. There is no network, database or server component in the default build; the only external integrations are subprocesses (decompressors, `--pre` preprocessor, hostname binary) and, under `unstable-index`, a redb embedded database on disk. Deployment is static binaries cross-compiled for ~14 targets by a tag-triggered GitHub Actions release workflow, plus a Debian package described by `[package.metadata.deb]`.

claims.claim: The single binary target `rg` is declared in the root manifest with `path = "crates/core/main.rs"`, and `autotests = false` with one explicit `[[test]] name = "integration", path = "tests/tests.rs"`.

`fn main() -> ExitCode` calls `run(flags::parse())` and dispatches on `args.mode()` into seven arms: indexed search, single-threaded `search`, `search_parallel`, `index::write`, `files`/`files_parallel`, `types`, and `generate`.

The workspace has ten members — `globset`, `grep`, `cli`, `index`, `matcher`, `pcre2`, `printer`, `regex`, `searcher`, `ignore` — sharing `edition = "2024"` and `rust-version = "1.96"` via `[workspace.package]`.
`crates/grep` is a pure facade that re-exports the constituent crates as `grep::cli`, `grep::matcher`, `grep::printer`, `grep::regex`, `grep::searcher` and (feature-gated) `grep::pcre2`.

The published crate names differ from directory names: `crates/matcher` is `grep-matcher` v0.1.9, `crates/printer` is `grep-printer` v0.3.1, `crates/searcher` is `grep-searcher` v0.1.17, `crates/regex` is `grep-regex` v0.1.14.

There is no persistent storage in the default build; the only storage layer is the optional `grep-index` crate, which opens a redb `Database`/`ReadOnlyDatabase` at a file named `index.db` inside a discovered `.ripgrep` directory.

`grep-index` is marked `publish = false`, version `0.0.1`, and is wired in only through the `unstable-index` Cargo feature (`dep:grep-index`), which the root manifest itself warns "may have very serious bugs".

Index code is compiled behind a `#[path]` module swap: `crates/core/index/mod.rs` selects `disabled.rs` (which `bail!`s "indexing not enabled in this build") or `enabled.rs` based on the `unstable-index` feature.

`build.rs` embeds the short git hash as `RIPGREP_BUILD_GIT_HASH` by shelling out to `git rev-parse --short=10 HEAD`, and on `windows`+`msvc` embeds `pkg/windows/Manifest.xml` via `/MANIFEST:EMBED` linker args to enable long paths.

Build/test commands are `cargo build --release` (optionally `--features pcre2`) and `cargo test --all`; CI additionally runs `cargo test --workspace --features unstable-index` and `cargo fmt --all --check`.
On musl 64-bit targets the binary swaps in jemalloc as the `#[global_allocator]` because musl's allocator measurably slows ripgrep down; this is the only allocator override.

Release shape: a `release-lto` profile (fat LTO, `panic = "abort"`, `codegen-units = 1`, symbols stripped) plus `.cargo/config.toml` forcing `+crt-static` for MSVC and musl targets so shipped binaries are statically linked.

The release workflow triggers only on `[0-9]+.[0-9]+.[0-9]+` tags, verifies the tag matches the `version = "..."` line in `Cargo.toml`, and fans out over ~14 targets including aarch64/armv7/s390x/powerpc64 Linux, macOS x86_64+arm64 and four Windows targets.

Packaging metadata installs `rg`, licenses, CHANGELOG/README/FAQ, plus a generated man page and bash/fish/zsh completions from `deployment/deb/` — artifacts that do not exist in the repo and must be produced by `ci/build-deb`.

feature_catalog.summary: ripgrep's user surface is a single command with a very large flag set: `FLAGS` in `crates/core/flags/defs.rs` is a static slice of `&dyn Flag` trait objects, each carrying short/long/negated/alias names, a documentation category, short and long (mdoc) help text, a completion type, and an `update` method that mutates `LowArgs`. Beyond plain search, the binary has distinct top-level modes — `--files`, `--type-list`, `--generate`, `-h/--help`/`-V/--version` special modes, and the experimental index modes. Output modes (`--count`, `--count-matches`, `-l/--files-with-matches`, `--files-without-match`, `--json`) select among three printers. Filtering features include gitignore semantics, `-t/--type` file types, `-g/--glob` overrides, hidden-file handling and `--max-filesize`. Provider-style integrations are the pluggable regex engine (`--engine auto|default|pcre2`), decompression (`-z`), arbitrary preprocessors (`--pre`), and terminal hyperlinks.

claims.claim: `Mode` enumerates the five top-level behaviors — `Search(SearchMode)`, `Index(IndexMode)`, `Files`, `Types`, `Generate(GenerateMode)` — with `Mode::Search(SearchMode::Standard)` as the default.

`SearchMode` has six variants (`Standard`, `FilesWithMatches`, `FilesWithoutMatch`, `Count`, `CountMatches`, `JSON`) and `HiArgs::printer` maps them onto `Printer::Standard`, `Printer::JSON` or `Printer::Summary` with a `SummaryKind`.

`--generate` emits ancillary artifacts: `GenerateMode::Man` produces roff, and `CompleteBash`/`CompleteZsh`/`CompleteFish`/`CompletePowerShell` produce shell completions, all rendered from the same `FLAGS` table.

`-h` and `--help` render different documents (`generate_short` vs `generate_long`) from `template.short.help` / `template.long.help`, interpolating per-category placeholders like `!!filter!!` and `!!output-modes!!`.
`--type-list` is implemented by `types()` in main, which iterates `args.types().definitions()` and prints `name: glob, glob` lines, exiting 1 if there are no definitions.
ripgrep ships a large built-in file-type table, `DEFAULT_TYPES`, mapping type names to glob lists (e.g. `ada` → `*.adb`,`*.ads`), extensible per-invocation via `--type-add`.

Three regex engine choices are supported: `EngineChoice::Default` (Rust regex), `PCRE2`, and `Auto`, where `Auto` tries Rust first and falls back to PCRE2, reporting both errors side by side if both fail.

`-z/--search-zip` transparently decompresses by file extension using external binaries: gzip, bzip2, xz (also for `.lzma`), lz4, brotli, zstd and `uncompress`, keyed by globs like `*.gz`, `*.tgz`, `*.zst`, `*.Z`.
`--pre` runs an arbitrary user program per file with the path as argv[1] and the file on stdin, optionally restricted by `--pre-glob` via `preprocessor_globs`.

Hyperlink support is a first-class feature with named aliases (e.g. `"vscode".parse::<HyperlinkFormat>()`) and interpolation variables including `{host}` and a `{wslprefix}` derived from `WSL_DISTRO_NAME`.

Sorting is user-selectable across four criteria — `path`, `modified`, `accessed`, `created` — with reverse variants; `HiArgs::sort` special-cases ascending path sort to be done during traversal instead of by buffering.

The experimental indexing surface consists of `--x-crud` (create/update/remove index entries), `--x-index-force` and `--x-index-path`, all in the `Category::Indexing` group, which renders as "Indexing is not supported in this build of ripgrep." when the feature is off.
`--stats` produces either a human block (matches / matched lines / files searched / bytes printed / seconds) or, in JSON mode, an extra `{"type":"summary"}` record with `elapsed_total`.

`ignore` exposes a second public feature beyond traversal: `IncrementalIgnore`, built via `WalkBuilder::build_matchers()`, which checks individual paths against hierarchical ignore files without re-walking the tree.

data_flow.summary: Input enters at three boundaries: `std::env::args_os()`, an optional rc file named by `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, and stdin (patterns via `-f -`, or the haystack itself). The parser folds all of these into a flat, dumb `LowArgs` struct through `Flag::update`, then `HiArgs::from_low_args` performs all the "expensive" derivations — compiling globs, building the type matcher, resolving the CWD and hostname, choosing thread count and mmap strategy. `HiArgs` is the single state owner for the rest of the process; every downstream object (`ignore::WalkBuilder`, `grep::searcher::Searcher`, the matcher, the printer, the `SearchWorker`) is constructed from it by a dedicated accessor. Bytes then flow file → `Searcher` → `Sink` → printer → `termcolor` writer, either directly to stdout (single-threaded) or into per-thread `termcolor::Buffer`s flushed by a `BufferWriter` (parallel). Exit status is a fourth output channel, driven by a match flag plus a global `ERRORED` atomic.

claims.claim: Config args are read from the file named by `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, one shell argument per line with `#` comments and blank lines skipped, then **prepended** to `std::env::args_os().skip(1)` and the whole CLI is re-parsed from scratch.
`--no-config` short-circuits before the config file is read, and `-h`/`-V` short-circuit even earlier via `ParseResult::Special`, so help output never depends on the config file or the CWD.

Each flag writes into `LowArgs` — a flat struct of ~60 public(crate) fields — via `Flag::update(FlagValue, &mut LowArgs)`, and by convention `update` only validates, deferring side effects (e.g. resolving `--hostname-bin`) to the high-level stage.

Patterns are drained from `LowArgs` by `Patterns::from_low_args`, which promotes the first positional to a pattern only when neither `-e` nor `-f` was given, reads `-f -` through `grep::cli::patterns_from_stdin()`, and de-duplicates patterns to avoid pathological regex compile costs.

`Paths::from_low_args` runs after patterns so all remaining positionals are paths; with none given it uses `grep::cli::is_readable_stdin()` as a heuristic to choose between searching `./` and searching `-` (stdin), and errors if stdin would be consumed twice.
`State` tracks one-shot derived facts across the low→high conversion, notably `stdin_consumed`, which is what makes the double-stdin error and the CWD heuristic consistent.
Thread count is derived once in `from_low_args`: forced to 1 when `--sort` is set or only one file is searched, else `--threads`, else `available_parallelism()` capped at 12.
Memory-map policy is decided from the path set: `MmapMode::Auto` only enables mmap when ≤10 paths are given and all of them are files; otherwise `MmapChoice::never()`.

Traversal output is `Result<ignore::DirEntry, ignore::Error>`, converted by `HaystackBuilder::build_from_result` into `Option<Haystack>`; errors are reported through `err_message!` and non-file, non-explicit entries are dropped with a debug log.
`SearchWorker::search` selects among four data sources per haystack in priority order: stdin lock, preprocessor subprocess, decompression subprocess, then direct `search_path`.

Search results reach printers only through the `Sink` trait (`matched`, `context`, `context_break`, `binary_data`, `begin`, `finish`); `search_path`/`search_reader` build a `sink_with_path` per printer variant and harvest `has_match()` and `stats()` from it.

In parallel mode each worker owns a cloned `SearchWorker` writing into its own `termcolor::Buffer`; the buffer is cleared before each file and printed atomically via `bufwtr.print(...)` to avoid interleaving.
In `--files` parallel mode output is funneled through an `mpsc::channel::<Haystack>` to a single dedicated printing thread, deliberately in place of a mutex.
Exit status is computed from two independent channels: the boolean `matched` returned by the mode function and the process-global `ERRORED` atomic flipped by `err_message!`, yielding 0/1/2.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows dominate: startup/arg-parsing, a default recursive search, and the file-listing path. All of them funnel through `flags::parse()` → `HiArgs` and then diverge on `Mode`. The parallel search path is notable because parallelism lives entirely in the directory walker — `search_parallel` just hands a closure to `WalkParallel::run` and never manages threads itself. The indexed path currently degrades gracefully: `index::read` opens the index and then falls straight through to the ordinary exhaustive search.

claims.claim: Startup order: `main` → `flags::parse()` → `parse_low()` which first calls `Logger::init()`, then `Parser::new().parse(env::args_os().skip(1), &mut low)`, then `set_log_levels(&low)` so `--trace` is live before config parsing.

If a config file yields arguments, the parser discards the first `LowArgs`, builds a fresh `LowArgs::default()`, re-parses `config_args ++ argv`, and re-runs `set_log_levels` because logging flags may have changed.

`Parser::new()` returns a `&'static Parser` memoized in a `OnceLock`, so the flag-name trie (`FlagMap` over short names, long names, aliases and negations) is built exactly once per process even though `lookup()` calls it repeatedly.
`HiArgs::from_low_args` begins by asserting `low.special == None` ("special mode demands short-circuiting"), which encodes the invariant that help/version never reach high-level conversion.

Default search trace: `run` → `search(args, mode)` → `args.walk_builder()?.build()` → `haystack_builder.build_from_result` → `args.sort(...)` → `args.search_worker(args.matcher()?, args.searcher()?, args.printer(mode, args.stdout()))` → loop `searcher.search(&haystack)`.

Inside one file's search: `SearchWorker::search` sets binary detection (explicit vs implicit) on the `Searcher`, then `search_path` dispatches on the `PatternMatcher` enum to the generic `search_path(m, searcher, printer, path)`, which calls `p.sink_with_path(&matcher, path)` and `searcher.search_path`.

`Searcher::search_path` → `search_file_maybe_path` first tries `self.config.mmap.open(file, path)` and searches the resulting slice; only if mmap is unavailable does it fall back to the incremental reader path.
The searcher has three internal strategies implemented in `glue.rs`: `ReadByLine` (streaming reader), `SliceByLine` (whole-slice, e.g. mmap) and `MultiLine` (when `--multiline` is on).

Parallel search trace: `search_parallel` creates a `BufferWriter`, an `AtomicBool` matched/searched pair and an optional `Mutex<Stats>`, then `args.walk_builder()?.build_parallel().run(|| Box::new(move |result| ...))` clones a `SearchWorker` per thread.

Early exit under `-q/--quiet` is implemented twice: the sequential loop `break`s when `matched && args.quit_after_match()`, and the parallel closure returns `WalkState::Quit`, which aborts the whole traversal.

Broken pipe is handled at three levels: inside the search loop (`break`), inside `bufwtr.print` (`WalkState::Quit`), and finally in `main`, which walks `err.chain()` for an `io::Error` of kind `BrokenPipe` and returns exit code 0.

Preprocessor trace: `search_preprocessor` builds `Command::new(bin).arg(path).stdin(Stdio::from(File::open(path)?))`, wraps it in a `CommandReader`, searches the reader, then calls `rdr.close()` so a non-zero exit code surfaces stderr as a Rust error.

Indexed search currently does no index-based pruning: `index::read` calls `args.index_read()?`, discards the handle into `let _index`, and then delegates to the ordinary `search`/`search_parallel` ("Do an exhaustive search for now").

Index discovery trace: `IndexDiscovery::discover` checks `RIPGREP_INDEX_PATH` first, then walks `cwd.ancestors()` looking for a `.ripgrep` directory containing `index.db`, returning `None` when nothing is found.

Man page generation trace: `generate()` groups `FLAGS` by `doc_category()` into a `BTreeMap`, renders each flag's roff via `generate_flag`, then substitutes `!!VERSION!!` and per-category `!!name!!` placeholders in `template.rg.1`.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is two-tier and unusually thorough for a CLI. Integration tests live in `tests/` behind a single `[[test]] integration` target and drive the real `rg` binary in a temp directory via a `Dir`/`TestCommand` harness; the `rgtest!` macro automatically runs every test twice — once with the default engine and once with PCRE2 — when the `pcre2` feature is on. Unit tests live inline in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` blocks, heavily concentrated in `crates/core/flags/defs.rs` (116 `#[test]`s, mostly per-flag parse assertions) and `crates/printer/src/standard.rs` (74). CI runs the suite on 18 build configurations including cross-compiled big-endian (s390x, powerpc64) and 32-bit targets, plus rustfmt, `cargo doc` with `-D warnings`, a wasm32-wasip1 build check, and a cargo-fuzz compile check. There is no coverage measurement and no benchmark job; `benchsuite/` is a separate Python/shell harness not run by CI.

claims.claim: The integration suite is one binary: `tests/tests.rs` declares modules `binary`, `feature`, `json`, `misc`, `multiline`, `regression`, plus `index` gated on `#[cfg(feature = "unstable-index")]`.
Test volume by area: `regression.rs` has 110 `rgtest!` cases, `misc.rs` 95, `feature.rs` 82, `binary.rs` 29, `json.rs` 9, `multiline.rs` 8 — regression tests are the single largest group.

`rgtest!` runs each test body twice when built with the `pcre2` feature — once via `util::setup` and once via `util::setup_pcre2` — which is why CI skips PCRE2 tests under cross/qemu to avoid doubling runtime.
`Dir::new` locates the `rg` binary relative to `env::current_exe()` and creates an isolated temp working directory keyed by a global atomic counter, so tests can create real files and symlinks.
`TestCommand::env` exists specifically so tests can exercise environment-driven behavior such as `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`.
Decompression is covered by committed fixture files: `tests/data/` contains `sherlock.{gz,bz2,xz,lz4,lzma,br,zst,Z}` matching the glob table in `default_decompression_commands`.
`cmd_exists` lets tests skip gracefully when an external decompression binary isn't installed on the runner, by probing `program --help`.

Index tests are split into `tests/index/basic.rs` (UX happy paths) and `tests/index/disallowed.rs`, the latter asserting that `-X` combined with `--files-without-match`, `--text` or `-Eutf16` errors out.
`crates/core/flags/defs.rs` carries 116 `#[test]` functions — largely `parse_low_raw([...])` assertions per flag — making the flag table the most densely unit-tested file in the repo.

Structural invariants of the flag table are enforced by tests: `shorts_no_duplicates`, `longs_no_duplicates`, `shorts_all_ascii_alphanumeric` and `longs_all_ascii_alphanumeric` (which also validates aliases and negations).
CI runs two informational tests with `--nocapture`: `flags::defs::tests::available_shorts` (prints unused short-flag letters) and grep-cli's `print_hostname`.
Shell completion correctness is tested outside cargo by the `ci/test-complete` script, which is skipped on Windows and on cross-compiled targets.
The CI matrix pins the MSRV build to Rust 1.96.0 and includes big-endian (s390x, powerpc64), 32-bit (i686, armv7) and Windows-on-ARM runners, so endianness and pointer-width bugs are caught.

Fuzzing is compile-checked only: the `fuzz_testing` CI job installs `cargo-fuzz` and runs `cargo check` in `fuzz/`; the sole target is `fuzz_glob` against the `globset` crate's `arbitrary` feature — the searcher and printer are not fuzzed.
Documentation is gated in CI: `cargo doc --no-deps --document-private-items --workspace` runs with `RUSTDOCFLAGS: -D warnings`, so a broken intra-doc link fails the build.

risk_map.summary: ripgrep has a small but real attack surface for a search tool: it executes external programs (decompressors, `--pre`, `--hostname-bin`), reads a config file from an environment-variable-named path whose contents become command-line flags, and memory-maps files it does not control. The codebase acknowledges most of these explicitly in comments — the mmap `unsafe` block calls its own reasoning "suspect", and `resolve_binary` exists specifically to stop Windows CWD-relative program resolution. The most fragile coupling is the 246KB `defs.rs` flag table, where a single flag touches parsing, help text, man page and four completion generators. The experimental index path is the least-finished area: `grep-index` opens with `#![allow(warnings)]`, its literal module is self-described as a prototype, and `index::read` doesn't actually use the index yet.

claims.claim: Arbitrary code execution is by design in three places — `--pre` (`Command::new(bin).arg(path)`), `-z` decompressors, and `--hostname-bin` — all spawned with the user's environment inherited.

`resolve_binary` is a deliberate Windows security mitigation: without it, `Command::new` hands relative paths to `CreateProcess`, which searches the CWD, so `rg -z` in an untrusted tree could run an attacker-planted `gzip.exe`. On non-Windows it is a no-op returning the path unchanged.

`RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` turns a file's contents into command-line arguments that are prepended to argv, so anything that can set that env var or write that file can inject flags including `--pre` — a full code-execution vector with no allowlist or validation.

The memory-map `unsafe` block carries an explicit hazard note: a file truncated concurrently with the search can raise SIGBUS and abort the process, and the author writes "This reasoning should be treated as suspect."

File IO is unbounded outside the repo root by nature — `walk_builder` starts at user-supplied paths with `follow_links(self.follow)` and `same_file_system(self.one_file_system)`, so `-L` on a hostile tree can be walked out of the intended subtree.
Index discovery reads `RIPGREP_INDEX_PATH` and otherwise walks every ancestor of the CWD looking for `.ripgrep`, a lookup the code itself flags as "subject to TOCTOU problems".
`crates/index/src/lib.rs` opens with `#![allow(warnings)]`, suppressing all compiler lints for the entire index crate — including dead code and unused results.

`crates/index/src/literal.rs` is self-described as "currently a prototype ... hastily written in order to bootstrap ngram extraction", so the ngram query construction (`GramQuery::And/Or/Literal`) is not production-hardened.
Indexed search is effectively dead weight today: `index::read` binds the opened index to `let _index` and runs a full exhaustive search anyway, so `-X` costs index-open time for zero pruning benefit.

`crates/core/flags/defs.rs` is 246KB — larger than the next two biggest files combined — and each flag must stay consistent across `Flag::update`, `doc_short`, `doc_long`, `doc_category` and `completion_type`, making it the highest blast-radius file for CLI changes.

`FlagValue::unwrap_switch`/`unwrap_value` panic via `unreachable!` on mismatch; this is intentional (a bug indicator) but means an `is_switch()`/`update()` inconsistency in a new flag is a runtime panic rather than a compile error.

Error reporting is global mutable state: three `AtomicBool`s (`MESSAGES`, `IGNORE_MESSAGES`, `ERRORED`) set once at startup and read at exit, so any code path that prints an error without going through `err_message!` silently fails to change the exit code.

`eprintln_locked!` calls `std::process::exit(0)`/`exit(2)` directly on write failure, bypassing destructors and any in-flight buffered output — an abrupt-termination path inside a macro used throughout the binary.

Sorting and parallelism are coupled by an assertion rather than the type system: `walk_builder` contains `assert_eq!(1, self.threads, "sorting implies single threaded")`, so a future change to the thread heuristic would panic at runtime.
The `FLAGS` slice order is load-bearing for generated documentation ("The order of these flags matter ... This is why the deprecated flags are last"), an invariant no test enforces.
`is_readable_stdin()` is documented as a heuristic with a "terrible failure mode": exec-process APIs that open an unused stdin pipe make `rg foo` appear to hang while it waits on stdin.

extension_points.summary: ripgrep's extension seams are almost all static tables and traits rather than runtime plugin systems. Adding a flag means adding one unit struct implementing `Flag` and one entry in the `FLAGS` slice; everything downstream (parser trie, `-h`, `--help`, man page, four shell completions) derives from that. Adding a file type means one line in `DEFAULT_TYPES`. Adding a decompressor means one `add(glob, ARGS, &mut cmds)` line. At the library level, `Matcher` and `Sink` are the two real trait-based extension points: any regex engine implementing `grep_matcher::Matcher` can be plugged into the searcher, and any output format implementing `grep_searcher::Sink` can consume results. The `ParallelVisitorBuilder` trait in `ignore` lets external callers drive the parallel walker with their own per-thread state.

claims.claim: The primary extension point is the `Flag` trait plus the `FLAGS: &[&dyn Flag]` slice; the module doc states the `defs` module "provides a single global slice of `&dyn Flag` values corresponding to all of the flags in ripgrep" used via dynamic dispatch.
One `Flag` impl can expose four user-visible names — short, long, `name_negated()` and an arbitrary `aliases()` list — as with `-E`/`--encoding`/`--no-encoding` sharing a single implementation.

`Category` (Input, Search, Filter, Output, OutputModes, Indexing, Logging, OtherBehaviors) is the grouping key for generated docs; `Category::as_str` returns the template variable name interpolated into help and man templates.
`CompletionType` (Other, Filename, Executable, Filetype, Encoding) is the hook a new flag uses to tell all four shell completion generators what to complete.

Four completion generators are registered in `flags::mod` as `generate_complete_bash/zsh/fish/powershell` and surfaced through `GenerateMode`; adding a shell means adding a module under `flags/complete/` and a `GenerateMode` variant.

`grep_searcher::Sink` is the output extension trait — implement `matched`, `context`, `context_break`, `binary_data`, `begin`, `finish` — and the crate ships a `sinks` submodule of closure-based conveniences (e.g. `UTF8`) for quick use.
`grep_matcher::Matcher` is the regex-engine extension trait; `grep-regex` and `grep-pcre2` are two implementations, and `PatternMatcher` in core is the enum that selects between them at runtime.

Printers are extended by adding a `Printer<W>` enum variant plus a `printer_*` builder in `HiArgs`; each variant only needs `get_mut()` and a `sink_with_path` method for `search_path`/`search_reader` to work.

New file types plug into `DEFAULT_TYPES`, a `&[(&[&str], &[&str])]` table of (names, globs) that the doc comment explicitly invites PRs against; users extend it per-invocation with `TypesBuilder::add`/`add_def`.

New decompressors plug into `default_decompression_commands()` via a single `add(glob, ARGS_X, &mut cmds)` call; unavailable binaries are silently skipped after `resolve_binary` fails with a debug log.
`ignore::ParallelVisitorBuilder` and `WalkParallel::visit` let external code supply per-thread visitors with owned state, as an alternative to the closure-based `run`.
`WalkBuilder::filter_entry` and `add_custom_ignore_filename` are the per-caller filtering hooks; ripgrep itself uses the latter to register `.rgignore`.
`HyperlinkFormat` implements `FromStr` with named aliases (`HyperlinkAlias`), so new editor URL schemes are added by extending the alias table rather than the printer.
`IndexDiscovery` is configurable rather than hard-wired: `env_name()`, `dir_name()`, `cwd()` and `create()` builders let embedders relocate the index away from `RIPGREP_INDEX_PATH`/`.ripgrep`.
The `grep` facade crate is the intended embedding point for third parties, re-exporting the whole stack under one dependency, with a worked `simplegrep` example.

agent_handoff.summary: Read `crates/core/main.rs`, `crates/core/flags/mod.rs` and `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs` first — they define the whole control flow and the low→high argument split that every other decision hangs off. Formatting is enforced (`rustfmt.toml`: `max_width = 79`, `use_small_heuristics = "max"`, edition 2024) and CI fails on `cargo fmt --all --check`, so run rustfmt before proposing a diff. Most changes that touch the CLI require edits in three coordinated places: the `Flag` impl, the `FLAGS` slice, and the corresponding `LowArgs`/`HiArgs` fields. Note the repository's `AI_POLICY.md`: autonomous agents are explicitly barred from contributing upstream, and AI-written comments to maintainers may be hidden — treat this repo as read/analyze-friendly but do not open PRs or issues on it autonomously.

claims.claim: `AI_POLICY.md` states "Autonomous agents are not allowed to be used for contributing to this project" and that PRs appearing in violation will be closed, possibly without notice; `CONTRIBUTING.md` says contributions not following it will be closed.

Read first, in order: `crates/core/main.rs` (dispatch), `crates/core/flags/mod.rs` (the `Flag` trait and `Category`), `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs` (`from_low_args` and every builder accessor), `crates/core/search.rs` (`SearchWorker`).

The core crate's own README warns it is not a library and is "glue code that brings the grep-matcher, grep-regex, grep-searcher and grep-printer crates together" — behavior changes usually belong in a `crates/*` library, not in core.
Formatting convention is strict and narrow: `max_width = 79`, `use_small_heuristics = "max"`, `edition = "2024"`; the `rustfmt` CI job runs `cargo fmt --all --check`.

Adding a flag requires: a unit struct implementing `Flag` (with `doc_long` in mdoc format), an entry in `FLAGS` at the right position for doc ordering, a field in `LowArgs`, and usually a matching field/accessor in `HiArgs`.

Per-flag tests use `parse_low_raw([...])`, a `#[cfg(test)]`-only helper that runs the parser once with no logging and no config file — the right tool for asserting flag parsing without touching the environment.
By convention `Flag::update` must only validate, never act: the trait docs use `--hostname-bin` as the example of work that must be deferred so it happens once, later.

Tests to run: `cargo test --all` for the full suite, `cargo test --features pcre2` to double-run integration tests under PCRE2, `cargo test --workspace --features unstable-index` for index tests, and `ci/test-complete` for zsh completions.

Integration tests create real files in a temp dir and run the built `rg` binary — they are not hermetic against the host, and `cmd_exists` gating means missing `gzip`/`xz` silently reduces coverage rather than failing.

Trap: `Flag::name_long` must be ≥2 ASCII alphanumeric/`-` characters and short flags must be unique ASCII alphanumeric or `.`; violating either fails `longs_all_ascii_alphanumeric`/`shorts_no_duplicates` rather than failing to compile.

Trap: changing thread-count derivation can trip `assert_eq!(1, self.threads, "sorting implies single threaded")` in `walk_builder`, because `--sort` and parallelism are mutually exclusive by construction.

Trap: in parallel mode the printer must not own the file separator — `printer_standard` only calls `separator_search` when `self.threads == 1`, because the `BufferWriter` owns separator logic otherwise.

Safe edit boundary: the `ignore`, `globset`, `grep-cli`, `grep-matcher`, `grep-printer`, `grep-regex` and `grep-searcher` crates are published to crates.io with independent versions and `#![deny(missing_docs)]`, so any new public item needs a doc comment or `cargo doc -D warnings` fails.

Release hygiene: `RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md` and the `#:version` marker comments next to each crate version are the mechanism for coordinated version bumps; the release workflow hard-fails if the git tag doesn't match `Cargo.toml`.
User-facing documentation that needs updating alongside behavior changes lives in `GUIDE.md` (usage guide), `FAQ.md` and `CHANGELOG.md` (90KB, maintained per release), not in generated help alone.
